claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterogeneous microstructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations resolvable by TEM or atom probe.
A physics-informed graph neural network combined with Bayesian uncertainty quantification can accurately predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
High-resolution microstructural images can be converted directly into latent descriptors suitable as inputs to a reduced-order mesoscopic model.
A multi-fidelity model can refine image-based predictions through Bayesian updating with sparse high-fidelity simulation and experimental data.
Image-derived descriptors can capture hierarchical heterogeneity and the spatial distribution of chemical fluctuations.
Hierarchical heterogeneity and spatial chemical fluctuations correlate with local stress fields and potential fracture-nucleation sites.
Elastic-modulus mismatch between phases can create heterogeneous stress fields, induce non-local plastic yielding and crack initiation, and enhance toughness.
Bayesian calibration of the reduced-order model ensures that elastic deformation, inelastic deformation, and fracture initiation are captured.
Uncertainty quantification enhances the reliability of machine-learning predictions for refractory high-entropy alloys.
Bayesian uncertainty bounds will flag microstructures outside the model’s training regime.
The proposed framework will reduce computation time by roughly one order of magnitude, from hours to minutes per prediction.
The proposed framework will reduce prediction-error margins by 10–20% relative to conventional multiphysics simulations.
Machine-learning models have demonstrated efficacy in predicting high-entropy-alloy properties, including yield strength and plasticity of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Prior evidence supports improved computational efficiency from the proposed image-based GNN and Bayesian framework.
The method is applicable to room-temperature tensile and fracture testing when microstructural features remain within the variability represented during training.
The method may become unreliable for out-of-distribution images, previously unobserved phase transformations, or previously unobserved chemical inhomogeneities.
Traditional atomistic, CALPHAD, and deterministic multiphysics approaches are computationally expensive and struggle to predict fracture toughness accurately.
The exact gains in accuracy and efficiency depend on training-set diversity and the precision of image-derived descriptors.
A blinded prospective benchmark will compare preregistered predictions against measured Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness for imaged HfNbTiVAl10 samples.
The hypothesis is falsified if any predicted property differs from experiment by more than 10–20% in over 30% of blinded tests, or if uncertainty estimates fail to flag large errors.
